text: severe protein malnutrition, organ or stem cell transplants, persistent CD4+ T lymphocyte counts lower than 200 cells/microlitre, or patients receiving cytotoxic or immunosuppressive therapy.2,10,11 Secondary prophylaxis is given to all patients following successful treatment of PCP.2 For both primary and secondary prophylaxis1,4,7 the drug of choice is: • co-trimoxazole Alternative prophylactic regimens1,2,4,7 for patients not able to receive co-trimoxazole are: • dapsone (alone or with pyrimethamine) • aerosolised pentamidine • atovaquone Other prophylactic regimens include intermittent parenter- al administration of pentamidine, pyrimethamine with sul- fadoxine, clindamycin with primaquine, and trimetrexate, but are not recommended unless the more usual drugs cannot be used.7 Co-trimoxazole has the added advantage of also protecting against bacterial infections and toxoplas- mosis, a common opportunistic infection in AIDS pa- tients.7 In HIV-infected patients, primary and secondary prophy- laxis may be discontinued in those who attain a CD4+ T lymphocyte count above 200 cells/microlitre on antiretro- viral therapy. Primary and secondary prophylaxis should be restarted in patients whose CD4+ T lymphocyte count falls to below 200 cells/microlitre, and in those in whom PCP recurs at a count of greater than 200 cells/microli- tre.7,12 A study of solid organ transplant recipients13 sug- gested that lung transplant recipients are at continued risk of developing PCP and prophylaxis should be continued indefinitely in this group. 1.
